analysis.one_liner: Bans the sale and transfer of handguns, allowing them only for police, military, and licensed pistol clubs.
analysis.headline: The bill had no cosponsors and never received a hearing or vote; it sat in a House Judiciary subcommittee until the 104th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have made it a federal crime to import, manufacture, sell, buy, transfer, receive, or transport a handgun, with exceptions for the military, law enforcement, government agencies, and a tightly regulated category of licensed pistol clubs where guns stay under the club's control. It would also have set up a voluntary buyback: anyone who proved lawful ownership could turn in a handgun and get paid its fair market value, or at least $25. It was introduced by a single Democratic sponsor with no cosponsors and died in committee without ever being debated.
analysis.who_benefits: Under the bill's own reasoning, people in communities affected by handgun violence. The bill's findings state that handguns play a role in homicide, aggravated assault, and armed robbery disproportionate to their share of guns, and that restricting handgun availability would reduce violent crime and gun deaths. People who wanted to turn in a handgun would be reimbursed at fair market value, with a $25 floor. The only civilians who could still use handguns would be members of licensed pistol clubs, which would keep the guns locked under a club officer's control when not in use.

how_it_helps.text: Would prohibit importing, manufacturing, selling, buying, transferring, receiving, or transporting any handgun, except for the Armed Forces, law enforcement, government agencies, and entities licensed by the Treasury Secretary.

The bill's findings declare that handguns play a major role in homicide, aggravated assault, and armed robbery disproportionate to their numbers, and that restricting handgun availability would significantly reduce violent crime and handgun deaths.
Would let anyone voluntarily deliver a handgun to a designated law enforcement agency and be reimbursed the greater of its fair market value or $25, upon proof of lawful ownership.

Would license pistol clubs at $25 per year, with mandatory conditions: all members 21 or older, no member legally barred from firearms, and club-owned handguns kept in a secure place under the chief officer's control whenever not in use.

analysis.who_pays: Current handgun owners and would-be buyers would lose the ability to buy, sell, or freely move their guns, and could only keep using them by joining a licensed club that stores the weapon. Handgun manufacturers, dealers, and pawnbrokers would lose the civilian market almost entirely. Taxpayers would cover the buyback's cost to the extent the $25-per-club license fees did not, and federal taxpayers plus the Treasury Department would bear enforcement and administration.
analysis.who_pays_short: Handgun owners, buyers, and gun makers

drawbacks.text: The bill would end private handgun ownership outside pistol clubs, including keeping a handgun at home for self-defense. Its own findings assert that handguns in the home are of less value for defense against intruders than commonly believed and that other means suffice, a premise many gun owners and lawmakers rejected.

It would do little in the short term about the roughly 76 million handguns the bill says are already in private hands: possession itself would not be banned, the buyback would be voluntary, and the bill's findings concede that more than half of handguns are acquired secondhand, so licensing new sales alone would not quickly reduce handgun crime.

The reimbursement guarantee is weakly funded: payments come first from the $25-per-year pistol club license fees, which would cover only a tiny fraction of the cost, with the remainder drawn from general federal revenues, and the $25 floor could badly undercompensate owners of inexpensive guns whose claimed value could not be verified.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill attacked a real problem — handgun violence — with the most sweeping restriction available short of confiscation, and its buyback and club-licensing structure showed an attempt to soften the transition. But the design had honest weaknesses: it left tens of millions of existing guns in circulation and usable by their owners, so its benefits would arrive slowly and depend on voluntary surrender; it banned home ownership and self-defense use outright, a cost to millions of lawful owners rather than only to the gun industry; and its reimbursement scheme was fiscally thin. Even a supporter would have to call it a long-term bet with real near-term costs imposed on ordinary gun owners, not just manufacturers.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Judiciary Committee and then to its Crime Subcommittee, where it sat without a hearing or vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Sidney Yates introduced the bill on March 5, 1996, with no cosponsors.
The House referred it to the Judiciary Committee the same day, and on March 28 it was referred again to the Subcommittee on Crime.
No further action was ever taken; the bill never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Handgun makers, dealers, and existing owners kept the legal status quo untouched: no sales ban, no club-storage requirement, and no buyback program ever took effect.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Gun makers, dealers, and handgun owners

for.name: Rep. Sidney R. Yates
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its only supporter in the House; no colleague cosponsored it.

against.name: Henry Hyde
against.what_they_did: His committee accepted the referral and sent the bill to the Subcommittee on Crime without holding a hearing or markup on it.

against.name: Bill McCollum
against.role: Chair, House Judiciary Subcommittee on Crime
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on March 28, 1996, and the subcommittee took no action on the bill for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; the bill's only signs of support were a single Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors, in a House controlled by Republicans.

industries.note: The bill would outlaw civilian handgun manufacturing except for narrow licensed and government channels, eliminating their core domestic market. Per the bill's own findings, handgun sales are the supply side of the violence the bill targets.

Selling, transferring, or brokering handguns would become a federal crime carrying up to 5 years in prison, and the bill's dealer definition explicitly includes pawnbrokers. Their revenue depends on the transactions the bill bans.

The bill makes licensed clubs the only legal channel for civilian handgun use, with members' guns stored under club control, giving clubs a protected franchise under a $25 annual license. Their interest survives the bill only because the bill's public-safety design routes all civilian access through them.
